historical_timeline.summary: A breast tumor proved benign; talk on silence to the Modern Language Association.
Found a lump in her right breast at self-examination.
Breast cancer diagnosed; mastectomy; declined a prosthesis.
Learned that the cancer had spread to her liver; chose alternative treatments rather than more surgery.
Named poet laureate of New York State.

claims.statement: Audre Lorde was born Audrey Geraldine Lorde on February 18, 1934, in New York City; her parents were immigrants from Grenada.

Lorde was a poet, essayist, and novelist. In her poetry and prose she wrote about matters important to her as a woman of color, as a lesbian, as a mother, and as a feminist; a reference biography describes her as an African American lesbian feminist and poet.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her identity is recorded as her published work and the cited sources describe it, and only in these terms.

claims.statement: In 1977 a doctor found a tumor in Lorde's breast that, after about three weeks of uncertainty, proved benign. In a talk given that year to the Modern Language Association she said: "Your silence will not protect you."
claims.clinical_interpretation: A benign breast tumor in 1977; the organ is not identified further in the fetched source. One biography dates her breast cancer diagnosis to 1977 (see the editorial resolutions).

source_links.locator: Gives 1977 as the year of the breast cancer diagnosis

claims.statement: On Labor Day 1978, during a routine self-examination, Lorde found a lump in her right breast; a diagnosis of malignancy and a mastectomy followed. She described the experience in The Cancer Journals.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented diagnosis that anchors the synthetic episode. Tumor type, size, stage, receptor status, and any treatment besides the mastectomy are not given in the fetched sources.

claims.statement: After her mastectomy Lorde chose never to hide the fact of her missing breast. She refused to wear the "wad of lambswool pressed into a pale pink breast-shaped pad" pushed on her by nurses and medical counselors, and she was repeatedly scolded for posing a threat to cancer patient "morale."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her decision about a prosthesis is recorded as her own considered choice and is respected in the synthetic episode.

claims.statement: The Cancer Journals (Spinsters, Ink, 1980), her first prose collection, combines journal entries from her hospital stay and recovery with essays; it won the American Library Association Gay Caucus Book of the Year award for 1981.

In 1984, six years after her mastectomy, Lorde learned that her breast cancer had spread to her liver. This time she chose alternative treatments rather than more surgery, and she wrote about it in the title essay of A Burst of Light.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Later than the synthetic episode and not used in it; her treatment choice is recorded as her own decision without comment.

claims.statement: A Burst of Light, published by Firebrand in 1988, won a book award from the Before Columbus Foundation. Lorde was the poet laureate of New York State in 1991 and 1992.
Lorde died on November 17, 1992, at Christiansted on St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands, at 58. Sources give the cause as liver cancer, the spread of her breast cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Provide primary care survivorship care for a premenopausal woman of 45 after mastectomy for stage IA hormone receptor-positive breast cancer: monitor adjuvant tamoxifen (vasomotor symptoms, abnormal bleeding, and clot symptoms), surveil the remaining breast with a yearly mammogram and no routine blood tests or body imaging, counsel on lymphedema risk and bone health, screen for distress, arrange the germline genetic assessment missed at diagnosis, and respect her informed decision not to have reconstruction or wear a prosthesis.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Lorde returns three weeks after her first visit here. She saw Dr. Lozano of medical oncology this morning. She has taken tamoxifen every day for five months. She has three or four hot flashes a day and is woken by one on one or two nights a week; she would rather manage them without another medicine if she can. Her periods continue every four to five weeks, a little lighter, with no bleeding between them. She has no leg swelling, chest pain, or breathlessness. The mastectomy scar is comfortable, and she has no arm heaviness or swelling. She is writing and walking daily and feels steady in mood. She is settled in her decisions after surgery: she chose a flat closure and does not want reconstruction or an external prosthesis.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Lorde returns three months after the consultation visit. She has taken tamoxifen daily for eight months. The cooling measures and paced breathing have helped: she now has one or two mild hot flashes a day and is rarely woken at night, so she has not needed venlafaxine. Her periods are regular and lighter, with no bleeding between them. She has had no leg swelling, breathlessness, bone pain, cough, or new lumps, and no swelling or heaviness of the right arm. She walks about 30 minutes most days and has been writing and giving readings. The genetic counseling clinic has offered its first appointment in early October.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Lorde comes for her yearly preventive visit, three weeks after her one-year survivorship visit. She is thirteen months from a right mastectomy for stage IA hormone receptor-positive breast cancer and has taken tamoxifen daily for a year. Her left mammogram four weeks ago was normal. She saw the genetic counselor two weeks ago, and the panel result is expected in about two weeks. Her hot flashes are mild and settled with the cooling measures she has used since the spring. Her periods come every 28 to 35 days and are lighter than before tamoxifen, with no bleeding between periods. She walks most days and is writing well. She completed the health risk assessment before the visit.

referral.question: Woman of 45, five and a half months after right total mastectomy for stage IA hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, on tamoxifen since one month after surgery and now moving her survivorship care to primary care at this center. Please review the adjuvant endocrine plan and advise on hot flashes, surveillance, and genetic assessment, so that we can share her follow-up
referral.pertinent_history: Right breast lump found at self-examination last September. Diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound: 1.6 cm mass, BI-RADS 5, normal axillary nodes. Core biopsy: invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, ER 90 percent, PR 60 percent, HER2 1+, Ki-67 12 percent. Right total mastectomy with flat closure and sentinel node biopsy: 1.6 cm, margins clear, 0 of 2 nodes, pT1c pN0(sn), stage IA; recurrence score 14. No chemotherapy or radiation. Tamoxifen 20 mg daily since late October. Premenopausal, with regular cycles. Mild hot flashes three or four times a day. No other medicines; no known allergy. PHQ-9 4, GAD-7 3. Germline testing was not offered at diagnosis. She chose not to have reconstruction and does not wish to wear an external prosthesis; she asks that this be respected and not revisited unless she raises it. She wants complete information and makes her own decisions
questions: Is tamoxifen alone the right adjuvant endocrine therapy for her, or is ovarian function suppression or an aromatase inhibitor indicated, and for how long?
How should her hot flashes be managed safely alongside tamoxifen?
What surveillance does she need, and are any blood tests, tumor markers, or scans indicated?
Should she have germline genetic testing now, and would a result change her care?
What should primary care monitor on tamoxifen, and how should we share her follow-up?

consultant_note.history: Ms. Lorde is seen at the request of Dr. Fairweather to share her survivorship care. She found a right breast lump at self-examination last September; a core biopsy showed invasive ductal carcinoma, and she had a right total mastectomy with flat closure and sentinel node biopsy at the end of September. She chose not to have reconstruction or wear a prosthesis, and this is respected. She has taken tamoxifen 20 mg daily for five months with three or four hot flashes a day, no abnormal vaginal bleeding, and no leg swelling or breathlessness. Her periods are regular. She has no bone pain, cough, headaches, abdominal pain, or new lumps. She walks and writes daily. She asked for the reasoning behind each recommendation
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Outside diagnostic mammogram and ultrasound reports; core biopsy and mastectomy pathology with ER, PR, HER2, and Ki-67; sentinel node pathology (0 of 2); the 21-gene recurrence score of 14; her medication list; and the PHQ-9 and GAD-7 from Dr. Fairweather's visit three weeks ago

assessment.display: Stage IA (pT1c pN0) hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative right breast cancer after mastectomy
assessment.assessment: Low risk of recurrence: small, node-negative, grade 2, with a recurrence score of 14, so chemotherapy is not indicated. Radiation is not needed after mastectomy with clear margins and negative nodes. For a premenopausal woman at this risk, tamoxifen alone is standard; ovarian function suppression adds benefit mainly at higher risk and is not recommended for her. An aromatase inhibitor would need ovarian suppression while she is premenopausal
Mild hot flashes, common in the first year and often easing. Medicines that strongly inhibit CYP2D6 (paroxetine, fluoxetine, bupropion) may reduce the activation of tamoxifen and should be avoided

For stage I to III breast cancer without symptoms, follow-up is history, examination, and a yearly mammogram of the remaining breast. Routine blood counts, chemistry, tumor markers, and body imaging do not improve survival and are not recommended. Breast MRI is for women who meet high-risk criteria

Testing is recommended for all patients with breast cancer diagnosed at 65 or younger, and she was 44. A pathogenic variant would change her surveillance (adding breast MRI and possibly gynecologic risk reduction) and would matter to her relatives; a negative result would leave her plan unchanged

recommendations: Continue tamoxifen 20 mg daily for at least five years, and consider ten years at the five-year review; no ovarian function suppression, aromatase inhibitor, or chemotherapy

Hot flashes: non-drug measures first (cooling, layered clothing, paced breathing, cognitive behavioral strategies); if they disturb sleep, venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily; avoid paroxetine, fluoxetine, and bupropion

Surveillance: cancer-related history and examination every three to six months for three years, then every six to twelve months to year five, then yearly; diagnostic mammogram of the left breast in September and yearly thereafter; no routine laboratory tests, tumor markers, or body imaging unless symptoms arise
Genetic counseling with multigene panel germline testing now

Primary care to ask at every visit about abnormal vaginal bleeding and symptoms of a clot, and to arrange a yearly gynecologic assessment; no routine pelvic ultrasound or endometrial biopsy without symptoms; no bone density test while she is premenopausal on tamoxifen alone
Lymphedema risk is low after sentinel node biopsy alone; check the arm at visits and refer to a lymphedema therapist if swelling appears
A written survivorship care plan by one year after diagnosis, with at least 150 minutes of activity a week, alcohol at or below one drink a day, and screening for distress at intervals
Her decision not to have reconstruction or wear a prosthesis is recorded; no further discussion unless she raises it
